newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU ministers reject beef package compromise.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers reject beef package compromise.

text.p: European Union farm ministers on Tuesday unanimously rejected a compromise to break a deadlock over measures to cut output and compensate beef farmers battered by the mad cow crisis, EU officials said.
They said talks were suspended until Wednesday when Ireland, which currently holds the EU presidency, would present a new compromise text, originally scheduled for Tuesday evening.
"Our intention is to keep trying to get an agreement," an Irish official said.
But prospects of success looked remote.
The crisis was triggered by a British government statement that the fatal cattle brain disease, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), could be transmitted to people.

"It's very difficult to see how we can get an agreement," said Gerard Kiely, European Commission agriculture spokesman. "Ministers are trying to spend money which doesn't exist. They are not dealing with the central problem of reducing output."
Ireland had suggested postponing cuts in aid to cereals farmers to help fund the beef package as well as easing a politically unpalatable reduction in production.
But member states demanded extra aid and disagreed over how production should be cut following a 15 percent drop in beef demand since the crisis broke in March.
British scientists last week provided more evidence that BSE was linked to a new variant of the human brain disorder, Creutzfeld-Jakob Disease.
"The draft compromise is unacceptable. It's provocative," French Farm Minister Philippe Vasseur said in a statement.

Vasseur, under intense pressure from angry livestock farmers in central France, said Paris would reject any compromise that did not compensate beef producers for income losses due to the consumer scare over BSE.
"We either move towards an agreement or a crisis," Vasseur later warned at a news briefing.
France, the EU's biggest agricultural producer, is demanding an extra 500 million Ecus aid to EU farmers, of which around 100 million Ecus would be paid to French breeders.
Vasseur said Germany and Britain were among countries that supported his demand.

But EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler has said no extra money is available and that the losses of livestock farmers, estimated at up to 1.2 billion Ecus in 1996, were more than covered by emergency aid agreed in June by EU leaders in Florence, topped up by national payments.
Looking further ahead, Fischler said that 1.7 billion Ecus of savings in the 1996 EU farm budget could not be transferred to next year.
The EU's executive says that s, notably for setting aside farmland, must be cut to finance the 1.3 billion Ecus ($1.6 billion) cost of the beef package.

But Germany, backed by all member states except Britain and Sweden, believes the aid cuts are unnecessary because savings can be made in the budget and advance payments to oilseed farmers in 1997 could be delayed to the next year.
An Irish proposal to cut the limit on the amount of unwanted beef bought by the EU into public stores to 550,000 tonnes, from 720,000 tonnes would also bring savings.
Most member states rejected key measures to cut output, notably the so-called "Herod premium" for slaughtering new born calves, saying it would provoke public outrage.
But ministers were divided over alternative German proposals to promote early marketing of cattle.
